title: The four schools and their imams
hook: Four scholars, four cities, one chain of teachers and students. Meet the people behind the madhabs.

screens.text: On Day 40 you saw that Muslims pray with small differences, and that all four schools are valid. Today, meet the people behind them. Their story is more connected than you'd guess: one of them was born the very year another died.

**What a madhab is.** A **madhab** is a school of *fiqh* (Islamic law): a careful method for reading the Qur'an and the Prophet's *sunnah* ﷺ and drawing rulings from them, passed from teacher to student for over a thousand years.
bubbles: There were once many such schools. Four lasted, because generations of students kept learning, teaching and writing them down [Yaqeen, What is a madhhab].

screens.text: Tap through each one, in the order they lived.

events.title: Abu Hanifa · Kufa, Iraq
events.text: Known for deep, careful reasoning. His students wrote down and developed his method. Today it's the largest school: Turkey, Central and South Asia, and many US masjids.

events.title: Malik ibn Anas · Madinah
events.text: Taught in the Prophet's own city ﷺ and wrote al-Muwatta', one of the earliest books of hadith and law. Valued Madinah's living practice. Strong in North and West Africa.

events.title: Al-Shafi'i · from Makkah to Madinah, Iraq and Egypt
events.text: Born the year Abu Hanifa died. Studied with Malik and with Abu Hanifa's students. Wrote al-Risala, a founding book on deriving rulings. Strong in Egypt, East Africa, Southeast Asia.

events.title: Ahmad ibn Hanbal · Baghdad
events.text: Studied with al-Shafi'i. A giant of hadith who stayed very close to the texts. The smallest of the four; strong in Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

screens.text: **A family tree of teachers.** Al-Shafi'i was born in the year Abu Hanifa died. He traveled to learn from Malik in Madinah, and also studied with Abu Hanifa's students. Then Ahmad ibn Hanbal studied with al-Shafi'i [Madhab map; Yaqeen].
bubbles: So the four schools aren't rival teams. They're one conversation, carried across generations, with deep respect for each other's learning.

screens.text: **Why do careful scholars reach different answers?** Many verses and hadith can honestly be read more than one way. A hadith might have reached one scholar and not another, or been judged differently. And each school weighs evidence with its own method.
bubbles: The Prophet ﷺ said a qualified scholar who works hard and gets it right earns two rewards, and one who gets it wrong still earns one [Bukhari 7352].

screens.prompt: A friend asks Keisha: "So which of the four schools is the right one?" What's the best answer?

options.text: "All four are valid ways of following Islam. I follow my masjid's school while I learn."
options.feedback: Yes. That's the mainstream view, and it's how she can get her questions answered consistently.

options.text: "Mine is right and the others are wrong."
options.feedback: Not quite. All four schools accept each other as valid, and you can pray behind an imam of any of them.

options.text: "None of them; I just pick whatever ruling sounds easiest."
options.feedback: Not quite. Scholars warn against picking rulings by convenience. Learn one way well from a teacher.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Abu Hanifa al-Nu'man ibn Thabit (d. 150 AH / 767 CE), Kufa; school developed by Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani; largest today (Turkey, Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia; common in South Asian and Turkish US masjids).
- Malik ibn Anas (d. 179 AH / 795–796 CE), Madinah; al-Muwatta'; the practice ('amal) of Madinah as a source; North and West Africa, Upper Egypt.
- Al-Shafi'i (150–204 AH / 767–820 CE); studied with Malik and with Hanafi scholars; died in Egypt; al-Risala systematized legal theory; Lower Egypt, Yemen, East Africa, Kurdistan, Southeast Asia.
- Ahmad ibn Hanbal (164–241 AH / 780–855 CE), Baghdad; student of al-Shafi'i; compiled the Musnad; close to hadith and Companions' reports; Saudi Arabia, Qatar. (All from [Research Notes - Core Essentials, Madhab map]; IslamWeb 86509.)
- Al-Shaybani also studied with Malik. Many schools existed historically; most didn't survive for lack of students to carry them [Yaqeen, What is a madhhab].
- Reasons for difference: most legal texts are open to more than one reading; different evidence reached or was weighed differently; different methods [Yaqeen]. A mujtahid who errs still gets a reward [Bukhari 7352].
- All four accept one another as valid; praying behind an imam of another school is fine [AMJA 78081].
- Q10 common ground (scholar question Q10): learn from a qualified local teacher; follow the masjid's practice while learning; don't pick rulings by convenience.

**Likely questions**
- *"Did the imams disagree?"* Yes, on many details, while respecting each other's learning; their students carried on both the disagreement and the respect. Don't invent quotes or anecdotes.
- *"Can I switch schools later?"* Scholars differ on how and when; it's a serious step done with a teacher, not by convenience. Route to the imam.
- *"Are there Muslims who don't follow a school?"* Some scholars hold that following one school isn't obligatory and that a layperson follows trustworthy scholars [IslamQA 21420]; others hold following one of the four is necessary [Darul Ifta Birmingham 135125]. Don't take sides; follow the masjid while learning (Q10). Avoid Salafi/Sufi debates (rule 11).
- *"What about Shia schools?"* Short and neutral: Shia Muslims have their own schools of law (most widely the Ja'fari); this program teaches the four Sunni schools. Route more to the imam.

**Escalate:** formally choosing or switching schools; sectarian questions (rule 11).

**Don't:** rank the schools; call any practice wrong; present the masjid's school as the only correct one; invent biographical stories.
madhabNote: This lesson is about all four schools. Screen 9 shows {{masjid.name}}'s school. If your masjid follows Maliki, Shafi'i or Hanbali practice, the same advice applies: learn that school well from your imam, and pray side by side with everyone.
